item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Tuesday, 6 October 2026
item.description:
Stargrace still cleared over 2 million gold in WoW despite barely posting auctions, with pets and cheap transmog finally showing signs of life.

Syp speed-runs a LOTRO housing cleanup, dives back into the endless Barrow-downs, and eyes Wolves of Mordor’s surprisingly early October launch.

Tipa digs into Malifaux 4e’s Rasputina vs. Shenlong matchup, GG1’s Map the Area strategy, and the annoyance of the newly broken iPhone app.

CrazyKinux breaks down EVE Online’s Caldari Navy Hookbill, focusing on scram-kiting, five-mid-slot flexibility, and fitting choices that actually match your plan.

Bhagpuss is deeply impressed by Neverness to Everness’s The Witch, a Salem witch trials story channeling The Crucible with unusual weight and respect.

Scopique untangles Star Citizen’s baffling pledge lockdown, where CIG now forces backers to freeze one game-access package as unmeltable and ungiftable.

Wilhelm wraps No Man’s Sky Expedition 23, a hefty 43-milestone anniversary tour through the game’s major updates that mostly samples features without too much pain.

Tobold likes Defenders of the Realm: Definitive Edition but worries its sluggish Gamefound campaign could land in the riskiest zone: barely funded.

Kelly talks candidly about down days and the coping value of reading, learning Python, and writing when heavier feelings won’t let up.

Anarchae shares a sharp links roundup on DRM-free ebooks, Twitch transcript privacy, gambling harms, labor failures, and more, plus some good job news.

Joel’s weeknotes bounce from a Penn & Teller: Fool Us binge to UNO, seafood, Land of Eem almost happening, and an accidental rom-com outing.

Warner weighs Apple’s coming Full Disk Access restrictions against AI-agent privacy risks and the collateral damage for legitimate Mac apps.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Monday, 5 October 2026
item.description:
Roger looks at why modernizing LOTRO is so hard, from decades-old code and player attachment to the strict limits of Lua plugins.

Azuriel argues Valheim’s exploration too often means slogging through RNG-gated boss clues and recycled biomes after the initial survival-crafting thrill fades.

Kimimi makes the case that Hydlide isn’t just influential 1984 RPG history; it’s still a brisk, dangerous, genuinely fun adventure today.

Ramen Junkie bounces through Fortnite FOMO, a Little Prince detour in Infinity Nikki, and bafflement at Final Fantasy XI’s old-school setup.

Emily vents about mobile games locking saved currency behind paid piggy banks, a monetization trick she finds pushy, wasteful, and immersion-killing.

Shintar is relieved WoW Forever’s regional naming should ease name sniping, but now every character needs a last name too.

Wilhelm runs through Fantasy Critic League week 40, with Toem 2 and Nighthawks nudging scores and reshuffling the publisher leaderboard.

The Chronicler rounds up teaching, strategy, and example-play materials for Plantagenet, highlighting its Wars of the Roses spin on Levy & Campaign.

Tan checks in with a hectic life update, a haiku publication, Nier: Automata progress, and Aristotle chats that eventually drift toward AI.

Cristian shares a simple photo post: ducklings at Lacul Gheorgheni for the100pics.

Bruce Schneier points to another AI-assisted crack of a historic cipher, this one from 1809 and tied to Napoleon’s nephew.

Dave Winer praises Claude’s code-reading chops, enjoys blogging with Frontier again, and says climate change is the bigger existential threat than AI.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Sunday, 4 October 2026
item.description:
Cliffski says Ridiculous Space Battles hits demo-to-Early-Access runway next month, after a solar farm detour and a very deliberate solo-dev embrace of generative AI.

Sey shares Malmö Game Week highlights, from community-focused talks to indie looks at MAREGROSSO and Seeking Home.

Margot rounds up a cozy week with Big Walk, Orbitals, Toem’s sequel, and Woodo while real life stays a bit rough.

Emily takes a delightful detour from Death Stranding into Marvel’s Guardians of the Galaxy, then wakes up baffled by a very affectionate Drax dream.

Wes mixes fan-translation scene notes with a look at PS5 emulation’s AI-fueled acceleration, and what that could mean next.

Wilhelm tees up another EVE Online Geminate clash, with Fraternity’s Golden Week timing turning a holiday into a strategic flashpoint.

Anarchae’s week mixes autumn reset vibes with Hyperion thoughts, Traitors watching, game grinding, therapy, and remembering Levi.

Roger pegs Celebrity Traitors as Among Us by way of a parlour game, where famous people confidently build bad theories from almost nothing.

CrazyKinux thinks the Neuromancer teaser nails the vibe, while keeping expectations cautious after past sci-fi trailer letdowns.

Brennan argues the internet isn’t the story but the setting, pushing back on lazy “internet novel” and discourse-first framing.

Warner says Apple Intelligence eating storage shouldn’t shock anyone, because on-device AI was always going to move the cost onto your hardware.

Andrew Plotkin says Apple’s UK age-verification web filters are wrongly flagging his personal sites, and there’s basically nothing he can do.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Saturday, 3 October 2026
item.description:
Syp is happily steamrolling Diablo III with a pet-heavy Witch Doctor, using it as a Blizzard-flavored stand-in while waiting on WoW Forever.

Frostilyte’s September gaming recap praises Fields of Mistria’s writing and hooks, then dunks on how mining drags its farming-game progression down.

Bhagpuss is enjoying Nivalis Nights but mostly wrestling GeForce Now screenshots, UI clutter, and the eternal problem of taking decent action shots.

Luna’s Spooktober backlog invite lines up creepy picks like Doki Doki Literature Club, Bloomtown, Slay the Princess, and more for October play-alongs.

Oya’s September recap mixes Dispatch, Spanish study, and Ace Attorney with PlayTranslate on the AYN Thor for a neat language-learning gaming combo.

David’s Sword & Dragon crew adds a necromancer, loots the dwarven city, and cleverly uses a throne to herd skeletons out of the way.

Wilhelm is back in Valheim 1.0, grumbling about broken achievements, miserable raft sailing, and a suspicious troll shortage that might be seed- or mod-related.

Tobold finds Transport Fever 3 fun and intuitive, with nice train-building hooks, but immersion-breaking anachronistic industries and a tutorial bug sour the ride.

Shintar rounds up Disney+ Star Wars watches, finding Maul: Shadow Lord surprisingly good while The Ninth Jedi spin-off still leaves Kara underwhelming.

Joel’s September wrap-up hits podcasts, movies, manga, TV, books, and games, with Final Fantasy IV, Emio, Blame!, and Lanterns leading the highlights.

Dave Winer likes AI assistants moving into real-world services, then revisits BloggerCon and RSS 2.0 to argue bootstrapping beats BigCo reinvention.

Magi kicks off OCtober, a daily original-character drawing challenge with rising time limits and a very clear no-AI-slop rule.

item.title: The Daily Blogroll — Friday, 2 October 2026
item.description:
Tipa bounces off rusty EQ2 controls but still gets intrigued by EverQuest Legends’ pre-ruin Nektropos Castle, with puzzles, traps, and deeply ominous dolls.

UltrViolet pokes at FFXIV’s post-Endwalker lore spiral, shrugs at WoW Forever, and frames the whole MMO roundup as one big mixed bag.

Kimimi digs into Knot in 3D on the Spectrum, a first-person Snake twist whose tiny premise still squeezes out real tension.

Ramen Junkie checks out Beast Box Infinity’s Sacred Power Robo, a four-beast combiner riffing on the Four Symbols with lots of tiny transforming charm.

Joar got pushed back to FFXIV by a Guild Wars 2 jumping puzzle, while World of Warcraft currently inspires little beyond logging straight back out.

Emily comes away charmed by Syberia’s vague old-school puzzles, Kate Walker’s journey, and the slow-burn mystery around automatons and mammoths.

Wilhelm heads from old Freeport to Faydwer in EverQuest Legends, fondly ditching the Sea of Tears boat for a safer translocator hop.

Kelly’s excerpt appears truncated, but it looks like a personal post rather than a game writeup.

Anarchae breaks down how moving, job gear, and long-delayed basics ate into savings despite a steadier financial footing.

Welsh Troll riffs on syntax highlighting, arguing modern coding themes often overdo color while older CRT-era restraint was easier on the eyes.

Bruce Schneier surveys campaign finance data showing US politicians quietly spending on AI tools like OpenAI and Anthropic despite public skepticism.

Cristian shares a translated tale of a smart vacuum that works, dies, revives after service, then promptly goes bad again.
